To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

galaxy catalogs are a valuable tool for prioritizing follow-up observations for the next generation of gravitational wave detectors and that catalogs with 75% completeness are sufficient to achieve this goal.

(1) the use of galaxy catalog can improve the probability that a wide-field follow-up will be successful by ~10% - 300%, and (2) catalogs with 75% completeness are sufficient for follow-up strategies to be competitive with strategies that utilize a complete catalog.

galaxy catalogs can be effective at prioritizing wide-field follow-ups for the next generation of gravitational-wave searches, but the effectiveness of the catalogs depends on their completeness and the field of view.

how galaxy catalogs may be used to improve the probability of follow-up success when searching for EM counterparts of GW events from compact binary mergings.
the utility of galaxy catalogs for prioritizing pointings in the next generation of GW/EM observations.
the utility of galaxy catalogs for following up GW triggers from compact binary mergings with wide-field telescopes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of a catalog is beneficial, but that it is not necessary to use a complete catalog, and that the completeness threshold for the catalog is dependent on the field of view.
galaxy catalogs are still useful in the era of advanced GW detectors, but that the utility of such catalogs will depend strongly on the details of the follow-up strategy.

galaxy catalogs can be used to improve the success rate of follow-up observations, but that this improvement is highly dependent on the completeness and volume of the catalog, the number of pointings available, and the size of the GW error region.

galaxy catalogs will continue to be useful for follow-up observations of gravitational-wave events, though the utility of catalogs is diminished for the next generation of GW observatories relative to current instruments.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of incomplete galaxy catalogs can still improve the efficiency of follow-up searches for GW signals from compact-binary mergers.
galaxy catalogs can provide an improvement in follow-up success rates for a wide range of scenarios.

galaxy catalogs can still be effective for prioritizing follow-up pointings, even in the next era of gravitational-wave astronomy, provided that the fraction of the sky covered by a telescope's pointings is sufficiently large and that the catalog is sufficiently complete.
